claim: Olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) produce a constant synaptic density across different glomeruli.
source: Olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) produce a constant synaptic density across different glomeruli.
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of Brp-Short puncta and neurite volume across five ORN classes (DA1, VA1d, VA1lm, DL4, DM6) showing identical synaptic density of 0.56 puncta per µm³ despite differences in absolute synapse number (Figure 1H-I).

claim: Each ORN within a class contributes nearly identical active zone number.
source: Each ORN within a class contributes nearly identical active zone number.
evidence: Supported by MARCM analysis showing discrete, periodic peaks in Brp-Short puncta distribution that can be fit by Gaussian relationships, with single-cell clones showing 19.75 ± 0.68 puncta for DL4 and 29.06 ± 0.95 puncta for DM6 (Figure 2).

claim: Active zones from ORNs, projection neurons (PNs), and local interneurons have distinct subglomerular and subcellular distributions.
source: Active zones from ORNs, projection neurons (PNs), and local interneurons have distinct subglomerular and subcellular distributions.
evidence: Supported by nearest neighbor distance analysis showing distinct mean NND values and clustering patterns: ORNs have 17% clustered puncta with mean NND 0.99 ± 0.50 μm, PNs have 7.9% clustered with mean NND 1.10 ± 0.44 μm, and LNs have 15% clustered with mean NND 1.18 ± 0.70 μm (Figure 3G-I).

claim: The correct number of ORN active zones requires the Teneurins.
source: The correct number of ORN active zones and PN acetylcholine receptor clusters requires the Teneurins, conserved transmembrane proteins involved in neuromuscular synapse organization and synaptic partner matching.
evidence: Supported by data showing ten-a mutants have 23% fewer Brp-Short puncta in Or47b ORNs compared to control, and this phenotype is rescued by presynaptic Ten-a expression (Figure 4D).

claim: The correct number of PN acetylcholine receptor clusters requires the Teneurins.
source: The correct number of ORN active zones and PN acetylcholine receptor clusters requires the Teneurins, conserved transmembrane proteins involved in neuromuscular synapse organization and synaptic partner matching.
evidence: Supported by data showing ten-a mutants have 23% fewer Dα7-GFP puncta in PNs, and ten-m RNAi in PNs phenocopies this reduction (Figure 8D).

claim: Ten-a acts in ORNs to organize presynaptic active zones via the spectrin cytoskeleton.
source: Ten-a acts in ORNs to organize presynaptic active zones via the spectrin cytoskeleton.
evidence: Supported by data showing: (1) spectrin immunofluorescence is reduced in ten-a mutants (Figure 6F), (2) RNAi knockdown of α- or β-spectrin in ORNs reduces Brp-Short puncta by 17-18% (Figure 6G), and (3) ten-a phenotype is not enhanced by concurrent α-spectrin RNAi, suggesting they function in the same pathway (Figure 6G).

claim: Ten-m acts in PNs autonomously to regulate acetylcholine receptor cluster number.
source: Ten-m acts in PNs autonomously to regulate acetylcholine receptor cluster number and transsynaptically to regulate ORN active zone number.
evidence: Supported by data showing ten-m RNAi in PNs reduces Dα7-GFP puncta by 23% (Figure 8D), phenocopying the ten-a mutant effect.

claim: Ten-m acts transsynaptically to regulate ORN active zone number.
source: Ten-m acts in PNs autonomously to regulate acetylcholine receptor cluster number and transsynaptically to regulate ORN active zone number.
evidence: Supported by data showing postsynaptic ten-m knockdown in PNs reduces presynaptic Brp-Short puncta in ORNs by 20% (Figure 9D), demonstrating a transsynaptic effect.

claim: Bruchpilot-Short (Brp-Short) localizes to endogenous active zones without disrupting morphology or function.
source: However, Bruchpilot-Short (Brp-Short), a nonfunctional 754-residue portion of Brp (Figure 1A), localizes to endogenous sites of full-length Brp (Schmid et al., 2008; Fouquet et al., 2009) without deleterious effects.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Schmid et al., 2008; Fouquet et al., 2009) and validated by colocalization with DSyd-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), requirement for endogenous Brp (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C), and immuno-EM showing 90.1% of Nano-Gold dots colocalize with synaptic densities (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Brp-Short can act as a reporter of endogenous active zones under binary expression system control.
source: Thus, under the control of a binary expression system, Brp-Short can act as a reporter of endogenous active zones without disrupting morphology or function (Schmid et al., 2008; Fouquet et al., 2009; Kremer et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating this property at neuromuscular synapses (Schmid et al., 2008; Fouquet et al., 2009), mushroom body (Kremer et al., 2010; Christiansen et al., 2011), and visual system (Berger-Muller et al., 2013).

claim: ORN synapse number scales with ORN axon volume.
source: In examining five classes of ORNs, we found that ORN synapse number, as indicated by the number of Brp-Short puncta, scaled with ORN axon volume (Figure 1H), which itself scaled with glomerular size.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing correlation between Brp-Short puncta number and neurite volume across five ORN classes (Figure 1H).

claim: Sex-specific differences in synapse number exist for DA1 and VA1lm glomeruli.
source: Moreover, the assay revealed sex-specific differences in synapse number for two glomeruli, DA1 and VA1lm, that coincide with known sex-specific differences in glomerular volume (Stockinger et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing significant differences between males and females for DA1 and VA1lm (Figure 1H) and citation to previous work on sex-specific glomerular volume differences (Stockinger et al., 2005).

claim: One Brp punctum is equivalent to one active zone.
source: While extensive EM reconstruction is not available for the antennal lobe (and thus, absolute counts of olfactory synapses in each glomerulus for comparison), the recent use of labeled Brp in the Drosophila visual system indicated that one Brp punctum is equivalent to one active zone (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent work in the Drosophila visual system (Chen et al., 2014).

claim: The distribution of Brp-Short puncta in DL4 and DM6 ORN clones exhibits periodicity consistent with quantal contributions from individual neurons.
source: For both DL4 (Figure 2C) and DM6 (Figure 2D), we observed that as clone size increased, the number of Brp-Short puncta appeared to increase in discrete steps of a similar size, suggesting that each individual neuron contributes an equal number of synapses to the glomerular average.
evidence: Supported by frequency histograms showing periodic peaks that can be fit by sum of Gaussians relationships (Figure 2C-D), with statistical analysis showing low probability (<0.00048 for DL4, <0.05 for DM6) of observing such evenly spaced peaks by chance.

claim: Individual DL4 ORNs contribute approximately 19 active zones each.
source: The DL4 relationship was best fit by a 4-term sum of Gaussians (Figure 2C, solid black line) with a value of 19.13 for the apex of the first peak, corresponding to the 'single cell' contribution of active zone puncta. This is in close agreement with our original data of 19.75 ± 0.68 puncta for single cell clones (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by statistical modeling (sum of Gaussians fit) and direct measurement of single-cell clones (Figure 2E).

claim: Individual DM6 ORNs contribute approximately 29 active zones each.
source: The DL6 relationship was best fit by a 5-term sum of Gaussians (Figure 2D, solid black line), with a value of 28.62 active zone puncta as the 'single cell' contribution, which is again in strong agreement with our original data of 29.06 ± 0.95 puncta for single cell clones (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by statistical modeling (sum of Gaussians fit) and direct measurement of single-cell clones (Figure 2E).

claim: ORN clones display nearly identical synaptic density regardless of their size.
source: All observed clones also displayed a nearly identical synaptic density (Figure 2F) regardless of their size, consistent with measurements in whole glomeruli.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data from MARCM clones of varying sizes (Figure 2F).

claim: ORNs contribute 1632 ± 22 Brp-Short puncta to the DA1 glomerulus.
source: Of the three classes of neurons observed, ORNs contribute the majority of the Brp-Short puncta (1632 ± 22) and were widely distributed within the glomerulus (Figure 3A,D), though with distinct voids (Figure 3D, asterisk) where the glomerulus lacked ORN neurites and Brp-Short puncta.
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements using Brp-Short labeling in Or67d-positive ORNs (Figure 3A, D).

claim: PNs contribute 1182 ± 24 Brp-Short puncta to the DA1 glomerulus.
source: PNs were the second major contributors of Brp-Short puncta within the glomerulus (1182 ± 24).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements using Brp-Short labeling in Mz19-positive PNs.

claim: LNs contribute 528 ± 54 Brp-Short puncta to the DA1 glomerulus.
source: Finally, local interneurons (LNs) contribute the fewest Brp-Short puncta (528 ± 54) of the three classes.
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements using Brp-Short labeling in NP3056-positive LNs.

claim: The sum of ORN, PN, and LN Brp-Short puncta (3342 ± 99) accounts for the majority of synapses in the DA1 glomerulus.
source: These three classes of neurons, when combined, provide 3342 ± 99 Brp-Short puncta per glomerulus. When the endogenous number of active zones is quantified using an antibody to endogenous Brp using the same image-processing strategy, DA1 contains 3849 ± 80 active zones (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data comparing sum of labeled populations to endogenous Brp staining (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).

claim: ORNs display clustering of Brp-Short puncta with 17% of puncta having nearest neighbor distance ≤0.75 μm.
source: For ORNs, these large clusters amounted to 17% of puncta that fell within this range (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by nearest neighbor distance analysis of Brp-Short puncta in ORNs (Figure 3G).

claim: PNs display less clustering than ORNs with only 7.9% of puncta having nearest neighbor distance ≤0.75 μm.
source: Indeed, only 7.9% of PN puncta were clustered by this metric (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by nearest neighbor distance analysis of Brp-Short puncta in PNs (Figure 3H).

claim: LNs display 15% clustering of Brp-Short puncta with nearest neighbor distance ≤0.75 μm.
source: Within LN neurites, Brp-Short puncta also displayed significant clustering (15%; Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by nearest neighbor distance analysis of Brp-Short puncta in LNs (Figure 3I).

claim: Ten-a is expressed at basal levels in all glomeruli.
source: Due to the similarity in partner matching mechanisms between central and peripheral nervous systems, and the fact that both Ten-a and Ten-m are expressed at basal levels in all glomeruli (Hong et al., 2012), we hypothesized that the CNS may use Teneurins similarly to the PNS for synaptic organization.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Hong et al., 2012).

claim: Ten-m is expressed at basal levels in all glomeruli.
source: Due to the similarity in partner matching mechanisms between central and peripheral nervous systems, and the fact that both Ten-a and Ten-m are expressed at basal levels in all glomeruli (Hong et al., 2012), we hypothesized that the CNS may use Teneurins similarly to the PNS for synaptic organization.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Hong et al., 2012).

claim: Loss of ten-a reduces Or47b ORN Brp-Short puncta by 23%.
source: Comparing wild-type (Figure 4A) and ten-a null mutant flies (Figure 4B), we found that Or47b ORNs in the ten-a mutant (Figure 4B) had 23% fewer Brp-Short puncta (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative comparison of Brp-Short puncta between control and ten-a mutant (Figure 4D).

claim: Loss of ten-a does not alter ORN axon volume in VA1lm.
source: Notably, loss of ten-a did not alter ORN axon volume (Figure 4E), despite affecting glomerular morphology (Figure 4B), which is due to the loss of ten-a in neurons of the nearby DA1 glomerulus (Hong et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of neurite volume (Figure 4E) and citation to previous work on partner matching defects (Hong et al., 2012).

claim: Loss of ten-a reduces synaptic density in Or47b ORNs.
source: As such, synaptic density was similarly reduced (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements showing reduced density in ten-a mutants (Figure 4F).

claim: Presynaptic Ten-a expression in Or47b ORNs rescues the synapse number phenotype in ten-a mutants.
source: Restoring Ten-a expression to the Or47b ORNs in the ten-a mutant (Figure 4C), but not to the VA1lm PNs that are innervated by Or47b ORNs, rescued the reduction in synapse number and density (Figure 4D,F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing rescue of Brp-Short puncta number and density when Ten-a is expressed in ORNs (Figure 4D, F).

claim: Knockdown of Ten-a in ORNs by RNAi reduces synapse number similarly to the ten-a mutant.
source: Further consistent with a presynaptic role for Ten-a, knockdown of Ten-a in ORNs by RNAi also reduced the number and density of synapses similarly to the mutant (Figure 4D,F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing RNAi phenocopies the mutant (Figure 4D, F).

claim: Knockdown of ten-m in Or47b ORNs does not result in any synaptic phenotype.
source: Interestingly, knockdown of ten-m in the Or47b ORNs did not result in any synaptic phenotype (Figure 4D–F), demonstrating specificity for ten-a.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing no significant change in Brp-Short puncta, volume, or density with ten-m RNAi in ORNs (Figure 4D-F).

claim: Ten-a mutants show a 27% reduction in T-bar profiles in EM sections.
source: Indeed, quantification of T-bar profiles showed a 27% reduction in the number of T-bars (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by quantitative EM analysis of T-bar profiles per unit perimeter (Figure 5I).

claim: 56% of T-bar profiles in ten-a mutants display structural defects.
source: In ten-a mutants, 44% of T-bar profiles appeared normal (Figure 5D,J). The remaining 56% displayed notable structural defects including continuous, multiple T-bars (Figure 5E), misshapen T-bars (Figure 5F), and T-bars that were detached from the synaptic membrane (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of T-bar morphology in EM sections (Figure 5J).

claim: Spectrin immunofluorescence in the antennal lobe is reduced in ten-a mutants.
source: We found that spectrin immunofluorescence in the antennal lobe was reduced in the ten-a mutant compared to wild-type (Figure 6A–B) while N-Cadherin, a marker of synaptic neuropil, was unaffected (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence measurements showing reduced α-spectrin and β-spectrin staining in ten-a mutants (Figure 6F).

claim: RNAi knockdown of α-spectrin in Or47b ORNs results in 17-18% reduction in Brp-Short puncta.
source: In both cases (Figure 6D–E), RNAi in Or47b-positive ORNs resulted in a 17–18% reduction in Brp-Short puncta (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing reduced Brp-Short puncta with α-spectrin RNAi (Figure 6G).

claim: RNAi knockdown of β-spectrin in Or47b ORNs results in 17-18% reduction in Brp-Short puncta.
source: In both cases (Figure 6D–E), RNAi in Or47b-positive ORNs resulted in a 17–18% reduction in Brp-Short puncta (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing reduced Brp-Short puncta with β-spectrin RNAi (Figure 6G).

claim: The ten-a phenotype is not enhanced by concurrent RNAi knockdown of α-spectrin in ORNs.
source: Moreover, the ten-a phenotype was not enhanced by concurrent RNAi knockdown of α-spectrin in ORNs (Figure 6G), suggesting that Ten-a and α-spectrin function in the same pathway to regulate olfactory synapse number.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing no additive effect of ten-a mutation and α-spectrin RNAi (Figure 6G).

claim: Dα7-GFP puncta are apposed to endogenous Brp puncta.
source: These puncta were apposed to endogenous Brp puncta, as revealed by nc82 staining (Supplement 1 to Figure 7), consistent with these puncta representing bona fide synapses.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing colocalization/apposition of Dα7-GFP with endogenous Brp (Figure 7C).

claim: The number of AChR puncta scales with glomerular size in PNs.
source: As with ORN presynapses, the assay revealed that the number of AChR puncta scales with glomerular size (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing correlation between Dα7-GFP puncta and neurite volume (Figure 7E).

claim: Sex-specific differences in AChR puncta number exist in DA1 PNs.
source: Further, known sex-specific differences in DA1, as seen in glomerular volume (Stockinger et al., 2005) and in ORN synapses (Figure 1), were also observed (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing significant differences between males and females for DA1 (Figure 7E) and citation to previous work (Stockinger et al., 2005).

claim: AChR puncta density differs between DA1 and VA1d glomeruli.
source: Calculation of AChR puncta density in PNs revealed subtle but significant differences across different glomeruli. In the VA1d glomerulus, the densities were identical between males and females (Figure 7F). However, these were different from AChR puncta densities in the DA1 glomerulus.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing statistically significant differences in density between glomeruli (Figure 7F).

claim: Ten-a mutants show 23% reduction in AChR clusters in DA1 and VA1d PNs.
source: In ten-a mutants (Figure 8B), the number of AChR clusters in these glomeruli was decreased by 23%, compared to wild type (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data comparing Dα7-GFP puncta between control and ten-a mutant (Figure 8D).

claim: Loss of ten-a does not affect PN neurite volume.
source: Moreover, PN neurite volume was unaffected (Figure 8E), so AChR puncta density was similarly reduced (Figure 8F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of PN neurite volume (Figure 8E).

claim: Ten-m knockdown in PNs phenocopies the ten-a mutant for AChR puncta number.
source: ten-m knockdown phenocopied the ten-a phenotype (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing similar reduction in Dα7-GFP puncta with ten-m RNAi in PNs as in ten-a mutants (Figure 8D).

claim: Ten-m knockdown in PNs does not enhance the ten-a mutant phenotype.
source: Further, this reduction was not enhanced by knocking down ten-m in PNs of a ten-a null mutant (Figure 8D–F), suggesting that the two function in the same genetic pathway.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing no additive effect of ten-a mutation and ten-m RNAi in PNs (Figure 8D-F).

claim: Postsynaptic ten-m knockdown in PNs reduces presynaptic Brp-Short puncta in ORNs by 20%.
source: Postsynaptic ten-m knockdown, however, reduced the number of presynaptic Brp-Short puncta by 20% (Figure 9C,D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data using dual binary expression systems to label ORN presynapses while knocking down ten-m in PNs (Figure 9D).

claim: The Drosophila antennal lobe is the first olfactory processing center in the brain.
source: Olfactory information is received by first-order olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) and is transmitted by ORN axons to the antennal lobe, the first olfactory processing center in the brain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Drosophila olfactory system organization.

claim: ORNs are cholinergic.
source: Given that ORNs are cholinergic (Wilson, 2013), an ideal labeling strategy would image postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Wilson, 2013).

claim: Dα7 is endogenously expressed in the antennal lobe.
source: We selected the Dα7 acetylcholine receptor subunit because it is endogenously expressed in the antennal lobe (Fayyazuddin et al., 2006) and it has been used to examine organization in the mushroom body, a higher olfactory center (Leiss et al., 2009a, 2009b; Kremer et al., 2010; Christiansen et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Fayyazuddin et al., 2006).

claim: Bruchpilot (Brp) is the major structural component of the T-bar 'table-top'.
source: The major structural components of the T-bar include Bruchpilot (Brp) and Rim-binding protein (Wagh et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2011), with Brp encoding the 'table-top' of the T-bar and Rim-binding protein comprising the 'pedestal' (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous structural studies (Wagh et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2011).

claim: Rim-binding protein comprises the 'pedestal' of the T-bar.
source: The major structural components of the T-bar include Bruchpilot (Brp) and Rim-binding protein (Wagh et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2011), with Brp encoding the 'table-top' of the T-bar and Rim-binding protein comprising the 'pedestal' (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous structural studies (Wagh et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2011).

claim: The T-bar is an electron dense structure that promotes vesicle docking and release.
source: In Drosophila, the primary unit of active zone architecture is an electron dense structure called the T-bar, a specialized formation that promotes vesicle docking and release (Wichmann and Sigrist, 2010) present at peripheral (Jia et al., 1993) and central synapses (Meinertzhagen and O'Neil, 1991; Prokop and Meinertzhagen, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Wichmann and Sigrist, 2010; Jia et al., 1993; Meinertzhagen and O'Neil, 1991; Prokop and Meinertzhagen, 2006).

claim: Teneurins are type II transmembrane proteins involved in neuronal development.
source: Teneurins are type II transmembrane proteins involved in neuronal development (Young and Leamey, 2009) and are disrupted in human neurological disorders (Aldahmesh et al., 2012; Psychiatric GWAS Consortium Bipolar Disorder Working Group, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Young and Leamey, 2009; Aldahmesh et al., 2012; Psychiatric GWAS Consortium Bipolar Disorder Working Group, 2011).

claim: Teneurins are disrupted in human neurological disorders.
source: Teneurins are type II transmembrane proteins involved in neuronal development (Young and Leamey, 2009) and are disrupted in human neurological disorders (Aldahmesh et al., 2012; Psychiatric GWAS Consortium Bipolar Disorder Working Group, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies linking Teneurins to neurological disorders (Aldahmesh et al., 2012; Psychiatric GWAS Consortium Bipolar Disorder Working Group, 2011).

claim: Drosophila Teneurins Ten-m and Ten-a regulate synaptic partner matching in the olfactory and neuromuscular systems via homophilic interaction.
source: Recently, we demonstrated that the Drosophila Teneurins, Ten-m and Ten-a, regulate synaptic partner matching in the olfactory and neuromuscular systems via homophilic interaction between elevated Teneurin levels (Hong et al., 2012; Mosca et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work by the authors (Hong et al., 2012; Mosca et al., 2012).

claim: Basal levels of Teneurins interact heterophilically at NMJ synapses to organize connections.
source: Basal levels of the Teneurins interact heterophilically at NMJ synapses to organize connections (Mosca et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Mosca et al., 2012).

claim: Human Teneurin-4 is associated with increased susceptibility to bipolar disorder.
source: However, as proper synaptic function is impaired in many neuropsychiatric disorders (Guilmatre et al., 2014) and human Teneurin-4 is associated with increased susceptibility to bipolar disorder (Psychiatric GWAS Consortium Bipolar Disorder Working Group, 2011), understanding how the Teneurins regulate central synapses is a question with clinical relevance.
evidence: Supported by citation to GWAS study (Psychiatric GWAS Consortium Bipolar Disorder Working Group, 2011).

claim: Mammalian Teneurins organize the visual system.
source: Mammalian Teneurins organize the visual system (Leamey et al., 2007; Suzuki et al., 2012; Antinucci et al., 2013; Young et al., 2013) and Ten-2 can serve as a ligand for Latrophilin and localize to synapses in cultured neurons (Silva et al., 2011; Boucard et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Leamey et al., 2007; Suzuki et al., 2012; Antinucci et al., 2013; Young et al., 2013).

claim: Mammalian Ten-2 can serve as a ligand for Latrophilin and localize to synapses in cultured neurons.
source: Mammalian Teneurins organize the visual system (Leamey et al., 2007; Suzuki et al., 2012; Antinucci et al., 2013; Young et al., 2013) and Ten-2 can serve as a ligand for Latrophilin and localize to synapses in cultured neurons (Silva et al., 2011; Boucard et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Silva et al., 2011; Boucard et al., 2014).

claim: PN connections likely synapse onto PN and LN dendrites.
source: These connections likely synapse onto PN and LN dendrites, as shown by electrophysiology (Kazama and Wilson, 2009), and are analogous to the dendrodendritic synapses between secondary dendrites of mitral cells and olfactory bulb interneurons in the vertebrate olfactory bulb (Urban and Arevian, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to electrophysiology study (Kazama and Wilson, 2009) and comparison to vertebrate system (Urban and Arevian, 2009).

claim: LN projections mostly fill the gaps in the ORN projection pattern within glomeruli.
source: When examined at equivalent optical sections, these projections mostly filled the gaps in the ORN projection pattern, consistent with previously observed results for neurites (Hummel and Zipursky, 2004).
evidence: Supported by imaging data (Figure 3) and citation to previous work (Hummel and Zipursky, 2004).

claim: Teneurins can regulate cytoskeletal architecture.
source: Teneurins can regulate cytoskeletal architecture (Nunes et al., 2005; Morck et al., 2010; Suzuki et al., 2014) and function at the Drosophila NMJ by organizing spectrin, a cytoskeletal component (Mosca et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Nunes et al., 2005; Morck et al., 2010; Suzuki et al., 2014; Mosca et al., 2012).

claim: Teneurins function at the Drosophila NMJ by organizing spectrin.
source: Teneurins can regulate cytoskeletal architecture (Nunes et al., 2005; Morck et al., 2010; Suzuki et al., 2014) and function at the Drosophila NMJ by organizing spectrin, a cytoskeletal component (Mosca et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Mosca et al., 2012).

claim: The majority of synapses labeled by Brp-Short and Dα7-GFP are ORN to PN synapses.
source: As these values are less than twofold different, this is consistent with the majority of synapses labeled being ORN to PN synapses (Kazama and Wilson, 2009; Wilson, 2013).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of Brp-Short and Dα7-GFP counts and supported by citations to electrophysiology studies (Kazama and Wilson, 2009; Wilson, 2013).

claim: The constant synaptic density of ORNs suggests an organizational mechanism that controls synaptic density.
source: Remarkably, despite differences in synapse number and ORN neurite volume, all observed ORN classes had a constant synaptic density of 0.56 Brp-Short puncta per µm3 (Figure 1I). These data suggested the existence of an organizational mechanism that controls synaptic density.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of constant density across different ORN classes despite varying absolute numbers.

claim: The primary job of ORNs is to convey information from the environment into the system as faithfully as possible.
source: This may further suggest that the primary job of the ORN is to convey information from the environment into the system as faithfully as possible, that all information is treated equally at this level, and that weighting computations occur downstream in the brain (Masse et al., 2009; Wilson, 2013).
evidence: Inferred from the observation of constant synaptic density and equal contributions from individual ORNs, supported by citations (Masse et al., 2009; Wilson, 2013).

claim: Weighting computations in olfactory processing occur downstream of ORNs in the brain.
source: This may further suggest that the primary job of the ORN is to convey information from the environment into the system as faithfully as possible, that all information is treated equally at this level, and that weighting computations occur downstream in the brain (Masse et al., 2009; Wilson, 2013).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ORNs have constant density and equal contributions, suggesting transformation occurs later, supported by citations (Masse et al., 2009; Wilson, 2013).

claim: Different classes of PNs may modulate how information is received by regulating the number of acetylcholine receptors.
source: The difference in PN AChR density as compared to the constant density of ORN active zones suggests that different classes of PNs may modulate how information is received by regulating the number of acetylcholine receptors. This can thus contribute to the transformation of olfactory representation by antennal lobe neurons (Wilson, 2013).
evidence: Inferred from the observation of variable PN AChR density compared to constant ORN density, supported by citation (Wilson, 2013).

claim: Variable PN AChR density can contribute to the transformation of olfactory representation by antennal lobe neurons.
source: The difference in PN AChR density as compared to the constant density of ORN active zones suggests that different classes of PNs may modulate how information is received by regulating the number of acetylcholine receptors. This can thus contribute to the transformation of olfactory representation by antennal lobe neurons (Wilson, 2013).
evidence: Inferred from the observation of variable PN AChR density, supported by citation (Wilson, 2013).

claim: Ten-a may be required for the maturation of synapses in the CNS.
source: Thus, Ten-a is required not just for the normal number of active zones, but also for their proper structure in ways both consistent with and beyond that of previous studies. Specifically, ten-a may be required for the maturation of synapses, as misshapen and undivided T-bars resemble immature synapses (Owald et al., 2010).
evidence: Inferred from observation of T-bar structural defects in ten-a mutants that resemble immature synapses, supported by citation (Owald et al., 2010).

claim: Target choice and synapse organization can be biologically separable processes.
source: Moreover, the fact that ORNs can be mistargeted but still have the correct number of synapses suggests that target choice and synapse organization can be biologically separable, even when they employ the same molecules.
evidence: Inferred from observations that partner matching defects (mistargeting) can occur independently of synapse number defects in certain conditions.

claim: Brp-Short requires endogenous Brp for proper localization to synapses.
source: Further, RNAi against a portion of endogenous Brp not encoded by the Brp-Short transgene in those ORNs resulted in a loss of Brp-Short signal at ORN presynapses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, panels B–C), though Brp-Short was still detectable in the cell body. This supports the hypothesis that Brp-Short requires endogenous Brp for proper localization to synapses; alternatively, Brp-Short could require endogenous Brp for proper trafficking to axon terminals.
evidence: Supported by RNAi experiment showing loss of synaptic Brp-Short signal when endogenous Brp is knocked down (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C).

claim: 90.1% of Nano-Gold particles colocalize with synaptic densities in immuno-EM of Brp-Short-GFP.
source: Indeed, 5-nm gold particles were observed to decorate putative active zone profiles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, panel D) in ultrathin sections of fly antennal lobes. 90.1% of Nano-Gold dots colocalized with synaptic densities (675 5-nm Nano-Gold particles out of 749 particles observed).
evidence: Supported by quantitative immuno-EM analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

claim: The discrepancy between labeled synapses and endogenous Brp may be contributed by synapses made by additional neurons not labeled by the GAL4 drivers used.
source: This suggests that the majority of synapses in the DA1 glomerulus are indeed made by Or67d-GAL4+ ORNs, Mz19-GAL4+ PNs, and NP3056-GAL4+ LNs; the discrepancy may be contributed by synapses made by additional neurons, such as other classes of local interneurons (Chou et al., 2010), atypical projection neurons (Lai et al., 2008), or potentially peptidergic neurons (Ignell et al., 2009; Carlsson et al., 2010), or may represent a slight underestimation by the Brp-Short assay.
evidence: Inferred from the difference between sum of labeled populations (3342 ± 99) and endogenous Brp count (3849 ± 80), supported by citations to studies of additional neuron types (Chou et al., 2010; Lai et al., 2008; Ignell et al., 2009; Carlsson et al., 2010).

claim: The Brp-Short assay may slightly underestimate absolute synapse number.
source: This suggests that the majority of synapses in the DA1 glomerulus are indeed made by Or67d-GAL4+ ORNs, Mz19-GAL4+ PNs, and NP3056-GAL4+ LNs; the discrepancy may be contributed by synapses made by additional neurons, such as other classes of local interneurons (Chou et al., 2010), atypical projection neurons (Lai et al., 2008), or potentially peptidergic neurons (Ignell et al., 2009; Carlsson et al., 2010), or may represent a slight underestimation by the Brp-Short assay.
evidence: Inferred from the difference between sum of labeled populations and endogenous Brp count.

claim: The larger number of AChRs detected compared to ORN active zones may reflect overestimation associated with full-length Dα7 overexpression.
source: The similarity between the numbers of endogenous Brp and Brp-Short puncta suggests that Brp-Short is a more accurate estimator of absolute synapse number. The larger number of AChRs detected in each glomerulus may reflect an overestimation associated with full-length Dα7 overexpression or that these are postsynaptic not just to cholinergic ORNs, but also other excitatory neurons such as local interneurons (Chou et al., 2010) or PN-PN chemical synapses (Ng et al., 2002; Wilson et al., 2004).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of Dα7-GFP counts to Brp-Short and endogenous Brp counts.

claim: Dα7-GFP may label receptors postsynaptic to local interneurons in addition to ORNs.
source: The similarity between the numbers of endogenous Brp and Brp-Short puncta suggests that Brp-Short is a more accurate estimator of absolute synapse number. The larger number of AChRs detected in each glomerulus may reflect an overestimation associated with full-length Dα7 overexpression or that these are postsynaptic not just to cholinergic ORNs, but also other excitatory neurons such as local interneurons (Chou et al., 2010) or PN-PN chemical synapses (Ng et al., 2002; Wilson et al., 2004).
evidence: Inferred from the larger number of Dα7-GFP puncta compared to ORN Brp-Short puncta, supported by citations (Chou et al., 2010; Ng et al., 2002; Wilson et al., 2004).

claim: Dα7-GFP may label receptors postsynaptic to PN-PN chemical synapses.
source: The similarity between the numbers of endogenous Brp and Brp-Short puncta suggests that Brp-Short is a more accurate estimator of absolute synapse number. The larger number of AChRs detected in each glomerulus may reflect an overestimation associated with full-length Dα7 overexpression or that these are postsynaptic not just to cholinergic ORNs, but also other excitatory neurons such as local interneurons (Chou et al., 2010) or PN-PN chemical synapses (Ng et al., 2002; Wilson et al., 2004).
evidence: Inferred from the larger number of Dα7-GFP puncta, supported by citations (Ng et al., 2002; Wilson et al., 2004).

claim: Ten-a is the postsynaptic partner of Ten-m in regulating presynaptic active zone number.
source: This reduction is similar to the proportion by which ten-m RNAi reduced AChR number (Figure 8D) and also to the proportion by which loss of ten-a reduced Brp-Short number (Figure 4D). This suggests that Ten-m is the postsynaptic partner of Ten-a in regulating presynaptic active zone number, and that the presynaptic Ten-a/postsynaptic Ten-m interaction that regulates NMJ synapses is conserved in olfactory synapses.
evidence: Inferred from similar magnitude of effects across different manipulations and genetic interaction data.

claim: The presynaptic Ten-a/postsynaptic Ten-m interaction that regulates NMJ synapses is conserved in olfactory synapses.
source: This suggests that Ten-m is the postsynaptic partner of Ten-a in regulating presynaptic active zone number, and that the presynaptic Ten-a/postsynaptic Ten-m interaction that regulates NMJ synapses is conserved in olfactory synapses.
evidence: Supported by data showing similar transsynaptic effects in CNS as previously observed at NMJ, and genetic interaction data.

claim: There is a difference in how Teneurins are used between CNS and PNS synapses.
source: There are, however, some differences between the CNS and the PNS regarding the Teneurins. While presynaptic ten-m has a minor role in synaptic organization at the NMJ (Mosca et al., 2012), our data suggests the lack of such a role in the CNS (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by comparison of ten-m RNAi effects in ORNs (no phenotype, Figure 4D) versus previous NMJ data (Mosca et al., 2012).

claim: At the NMJ, Teneurin perturbations reduce active zone and synaptic bouton numbers but do not alter active zone density.
source: Interestingly, at the NMJ, Teneurin perturbations reduced active zone and synaptic bouton numbers, but did not alter active zone density (TM, unpublished observations).
evidence: Supported by unpublished observations cited in the text.

claim: In ORNs, Teneurin perturbation reduces active zone density because neurite volume is unchanged.
source: However, in ORNs, neurite volume was unchanged, so active zone density was reduced, suggesting a difference in the specific consequence of Teneurin perturbation in the CNS compared with the NMJ.
evidence: Supported by data showing unchanged neurite volume but reduced puncta number in ten-a mutants (Figure 4E, D).

claim: The 27% reduction in T-bars by EM is consistent with the 23% reduction measured by Brp-Short assay.
source: Indeed, quantification of T-bar profiles showed a 27% reduction in the number of T-bars (Figure 5I). This is consistent with the results from the Brp-Short assay (Figure 4D), which shows a 23% reduction.
evidence: Supported by comparison of EM quantification (Figure 5I) to confocal Brp-Short quantification (Figure 4D).

claim: The slight difference between EM and confocal measurements may reflect an under-report of the phenotype by confocal analysis or differences in which synapses are counted.
source: The slight difference may reflect an under-report of the phenotype by our confocal-level analysis or may reflect the fact that the EM analysis does not differentiate between ORN, PN, and LN presynapses while the Brp-Short assay does.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of methodologies and their limitations.

claim: The largely similar magnitude of synapse reduction in EM and confocal studies supports the validity of the Brp-Short assay.
source: The largely similar magnitude of synapse reduction in EM and confocal studies supports the validity of the Brp-Short assay, and further substantiates that Ten-a is required for proper synapse number in the CNS.
evidence: Supported by comparison of independent methods (EM and confocal) yielding similar results.

claim: T-bar defects in ten-a mutants resemble those observed at ten-a mutant NMJs.
source: These defects resembled those observed at ten-a mutant NMJs (Mosca et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by comparison to previous EM observations at NMJ, citation (Mosca et al., 2012).

claim: Continuous, electron-dense material resembling undivided T-bars was observed in ten-a mutants but not found previously at NMJs.
source: We also observed continuous, electron-dense material resembling undivided T-bars (Figure 5H) that was not found previously.
evidence: Supported by EM observations (Figure 5H) and comparison to previous studies.

claim: α-spectrin and β-spectrin function as a heterotetramer.
source: This was observed for α- and β-spectrin (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, panels A–D), which function as a heterotetramer (Machnicka et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on spectrin structure (Machnicka et al., 2014).

claim: The NP3056-GAL4 line includes most ipsilateral LNs including most or all pan-glomerular projections.
source: The LNs accessed by the NP3056-GAL4 line make up the majority of ipsilateral LNs including most or all pan-glomerular projections (Chou et al., 2010), but may not be representative of all classes of LNs.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous characterization of this GAL4 line (Chou et al., 2010).

claim: Mz19-GAL4 does not label all PNs that innervate DA1 and VA1d.
source: This variation can be due to technical caveats, such as Mz19-GAL4 does not label all PNs that innervate DA1 and VA1d (Jefferis et al., 2001; Liang et al., 2013), or that Dα7-GFP clusters do not reflect the absolute number of AChRs.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous characterization of Mz19-GAL4 (Jefferis et al., 2001; Liang et al., 2013).

claim: Dα7-GFP clusters may not reflect the absolute number of AChRs.
source: This variation can be due to technical caveats, such as Mz19-GAL4 does not label all PNs that innervate DA1 and VA1d (Jefferis et al., 2001; Liang et al., 2013), or that Dα7-GFP clusters do not reflect the absolute number of AChRs.
evidence: Acknowledged as a potential technical limitation of the assay.

claim: Postsynaptic PN AChRs may already reflect a transformed olfactory representation compared to output synapses of ORNs.
source: As the relative numbers still show these differences, an interesting possibility suggested by these results is that postsynaptic PN AChRs already reflect a transformed olfactory representation compared to output synapses of ORNs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of variable PN AChR density despite constant ORN density.
